module_title: Landmark Supreme Court Judgments: The Classic Pillars
introduction: This foundational level covers the undisputed classics of Indian constitutional history. These are the judgments that permanently shaped the balance of power between the Parliament and the Judiciary, redefined the Right to Life, and established the framework for affirmative action.

core_concepts.title: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
core_concepts.description:
The most important judgment in Indian history, delivered by a massive 13-judge bench (the largest ever).
- The Issue: Can the Parliament amend *any* part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, under Article 368?
- The Judgment: The Supreme Court ruled (7-6 majority) that while Parliament has wide powers to amend the Constitution, it CANNOT alter or destroy its **'Basic Structure'** (e.g., secularism, democracy, judicial review, separation of powers). This doctrine saved Indian democracy from legislative absolutism.

core_concepts.title: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)
core_concepts.description:
The judgment that transformed Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).
- The Issue: Maneka Gandhi's passport was impounded without giving her a reason or a hearing.
- The Judgment: The Court ruled that the 'procedure established by law' under Article 21 must be **just, fair, and reasonable**, effectively importing the American concept of 'Due Process'. It established the 'Golden Triangle' (Articles 14, 19, and 21), ruling that a law depriving a person of liberty must pass the test of all three.

core_concepts.title: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
core_concepts.description:
The 'Mandal Commission' Case.
- The Issue: The constitutional validity of providing 27% reservation to Other Backward Classes (OBCs).
- The Judgment: A 9-judge bench upheld the 27% OBC reservation but established strict boundaries: (1) Total reservations MUST NOT exceed **50%**, (2) The **'Creamy Layer'** (socially and economically advanced members) within OBCs must be excluded, and (3) Reservations are confined to initial appointments, not promotions (though this was later amended by Parliament).

core_concepts.title: Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997)
core_concepts.description:
A landmark instance of judicial activism protecting women's rights.
- The Issue: The brutal gang rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker, highlighting the absence of laws protecting women from sexual harassment at workplaces.
- The Judgment: Utilizing international treaties (CEDAW), the Supreme Court laid down the legally binding **'Vishaka Guidelines'** to prevent and redress workplace sexual harassment, which served as law until the POSH Act was passed in 2013.

important_entities.name: The Basic Structure Doctrine
important_entities.key_fact: An implied limitation on Parliament's amending power.
important_entities.significance: Before 1973, Parliament believed it could rewrite the entire Constitution. The Basic Structure Doctrine established that the Constitution has an unchangeable 'soul'. If a constitutional amendment damages this soul, the Supreme Court will strike it down (e.g., the striking down of the NJAC via the 99th Amendment in 2015).

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: Examiners often ask: 'In which Article is the Basic Structure defined?' **NOWHERE**. The Basic Structure Doctrine is not mentioned anywhere in the text of the Constitution. It is a purely judicial invention created by the Supreme Court in the Kesavananda Bharati case.

mnemonics_and_tricks.memory_phrase: Kesavananda = Basic Structure; Maneka = Due Process; Sawhney = 50% Cap; Vishaka = Workplace Harassment.
mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: Link the name directly to its most heavily tested legacy.

exam_strategy_tips: Whenever a Judiciary question asks 'Which case established the inter-relationship between Articles 14, 19, and 21 (The Golden Triangle)?', select **Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India**.
